author: David Njagi
title: The tensions playing out in Kenya’s marine conservation
content:
Mombasa, Kenya:

 Khadija Dossa charmed a group of visitors at her village in Wasini Island in Kenya’s coastal region with tales of how conserving coral reefs was improving livelihoods in her community. When she finally delivered her message however, it was clear there were gaps that needed mending.




Dossa belongs to the Mkwiro Beach Management Unit (BMU), and along conserving coral reefs, her group also farms octopus and seaweed while restoring mangroves. The investment has created jobs for hundreds of youth in the island struggling with unemployment after completing school.




It has come with the price of having to abandon the community’s long-held tradition of fishing freely whenever they liked and whenever it pleased them. During the free reigning days, Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) that restrict unauthorized access by communities did not exist.




“The ocean has provided us with food and a source of income from fish sales for generations and has a cultural connection to our people,” said Dossa, referring to the Swahili people who settled on the country’s coastal region.




In recent years, the world has united around creation of MPAs not just to protect coral reefs, but also to battle unsustainable fishing, water pollution and climate change, threats that were pitched to Dossa’s community by the government to convince locals to join the ocean conservation wave.

author: Carmen Esselink
title: Cape Verde’s Elections Were Loud. Its Voters Are Increasingly Silent
content:
On the 29th of October, before 10 o’clock in the morning, a car with speakers has already driven twice through my neighbourhood in Mindelo, the city of Cesária Évora and of Cape Verde’s best-known Carnival, blasting MpD (

Movimento para a Democracia, 

Movement for Democracy) viewpoints and a jingle. I notice I’m immediately annoyed, because I’m trying to conduct an interview from home and the noise keeps interrupting the conversation. The same car passes twice more that day. Three days later, on Sunday 1 November, a whole procession of floats drives along the beach, honking, accompanied by Cape Verdean and PAICV (

Partido Africano da Independência de Cabo Verde

, African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde) flags, candidate headshots and more jingles, while my boyfriend and I are trying to get onto the road in the car. Election season in Cape Verde has begun: a very loud time, and a disruptive one. As an outsider, I wonder whether it has the desired effect, people voting for a certain party, or the opposite: abstention.




The noise is meant to bring people to the polls. In May’s parliamentary election, most of them stayed home. Just 

46.5 percent of the 416,096 registered voters

author: Farai Shawn Matiashe
title: Electrification in Africa means closing the energy access gap and reducing energy poverty
content:
At the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, the COP31 presidency is pushing for a global target to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 

35% by 2035

, a central pillar of the conference.




The COP31 Turkish presidency proposed the global electrification target at the 2026 Bonn Climate Change Conference in June to encourage countries and businesses worldwide to electrify transport, buildings, and industry using renewable energy, helping to accelerate the shift away from fossil fuels.




But as delegates gather in the Mediterranean country for the climate summit known as Conference of the Parties 31 (COP31), the target risks overlooking the different energy realities Africa faces unless they place energy access and development at its centre.




For industrialised economies, electrification is all about replacing existing fossil fuel systems, while in Africa, some countries still want to build electricity infrastructure and distribution networks.




The new target, up from the current global rate of electrification of about 20%, comes at a time when Africa faces energy poverty and a huge electricity access gap.




About 600 million people lack electricity access, with half of them living in three countries, namely Nigeria, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo, 

according

 to the International Energy Agency.

author: James Hamill
title: A Disaster Waiting to Happen?  Brent Bozell and the US-South Africa Relationship
content:
President Donald Trump’s appointment of Leo Brent Bozell as the United States ambassador to South Africa in 2025 was a deliberately provocative act on his part. The appointment always seemed purposely designed to further damage a US-South Africa bilateral relationship which was already fraught due to differences over South Africa’s domestic and foreign policy choices. Put bluntly, for decades Bozell has been a conservative activist not a diplomat and he lacks the basic skills set to hold such an important and sensitive position Trump appoints Leo Brent Bozell III, a defender of apartheid in the 1980s, as ambassador to South Africa | U.S. | EL PAÍS English. As his behaviour in South Africa is demonstrating, that is an environment likely to produce partisan ideologues rather than people with the tact, nuance, patience, and knowledge required for high level inter-state diplomacy. Since taking up the role of US ambassador in February 2026, he has consistently abused his position through hostile posturing and ‘megaphone diplomacy.’ He has disrespected South Africa’s independent judiciary, publicly berated the host government, and has persistently interfered in South African domestic politics – in clear violation of Article 41.1 of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961– by aligning himself with Afrikaner nationalist groupings, Afriforum and Solidarity, and amplifying their grievances Between candour and coercion — why SA won’t bend to Washington’s dictates. He has issued a series of ‘asks’ – US demands in effect – on issues such as farm murders and rural crime, Black Economic Empowerment, land expropriation without compensation in exceptional circumstances US to make SA to pay the price of doing nothing. Consequently, he has now been démarched – summoned to receive a diplomatic reprimand – by the South African Department of International Relations and Co-operation on no less than three separate occasions in 2026: in March (after less than one month in position), June and September Dirco summons US ambassador Bozell again over ‘undiplomatic conduct’.

Bozell’s ‘extraordinary experience’ All of this was very predictable. Bozell’s appointment has captured in microcosm the broader failings of the Trump administration’s approach to diplomacy and international relations: it was incendiary and was designed primarily to appease white nationalist opinion within Trump’s MAGA base rather than to help mend US-South African relations. In a reversal of standard diplomatic practice, Bozell was sent to South Africa to exacerbate rather than ease tensions and to promote discord. Although Trump stated that Bozell brought ‘extraordinary experience’ to his role Trump appoints Leo Brent Bozell III, a defender of apartheid in the 1980s, as ambassador to South Africa | U.S. | EL PAÍS English, it is actually his South African ‘experience’ which is the main problem. Bozell has a long history of opposition to the African National Congress (ANC) whom he labelled ‘terrorists’ during the 1980s liberation struggle era. He enlisted his National Conservative Political Action Committee in a so-called ‘Coalition Against ANC Terrorism’, a collection of American conservative groupings supportive of the apartheid regime. He strongly opposed the US’s opening of formal diplomatic contacts with the ANC, initiated by then Secretary of State George Shultz in January 1987, in which the Reagan administration effectively acknowledged that there could be no long term South African settlement without its involvement Trump’s Pick For Ambassador To South Africa Actively Opposed Fight To End Apartheid. Bozell was also hostile to the liberation struggle per se as was demonstrated by his support in the 1980s for the regime of President P W Botha, his opposition to the global anti-apartheid movement, and his opposition to the US sanctions contained in the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act (CAAA) of October 1986. The CAAA proved to be of crucial importance in intensifying pressure on the regime and helping to move South Africa beyond apartheid. Anyone doubting its impact need only look at the striking similarity between the US demands, as set out in the CAAA, and the changes announced by President F W De Klerk in his historic speech of 2nd February 1990, over three years later. Bozell was profoundly wrong on everything South Africa-related in the 1980s: wrong to attempt to shore up a failing Botha regime which was leading the country to destruction, wrong to oppose US sanctions, and wrong in his animus towards the most important liberation movement, the ANC. Had Bozell’s approach prevailed, South Africa’s post-Botha breakthrough in 1989-90 would have been delayed and the country would have continued along a path of terminal political and economic decline. His prejudices were advertised again when he bemoaned the ‘mythologizing’ of Nelson Mandela following the iconic former president’s death in 2013 Trump’s Pick For Ambassador To South Africa Actively Opposed Fight To End Apartheid. Causing offence Appointing someone with such a track record to the post of US ambassador to South Africa, a country in which the ANC is the largest party in a government of national unity, was designed to cause offence and provided legitimate grounds for South Africa to refuse Bozell agrément under Article 4.2 of the 1961 Vienna Convention Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961. By choosing not to do so, South Africa was taking a more conciliatory approach, opting to look forward not back and signalling its openness to a genuine bilateral dialogue. This stood in marked contrast to the Trump administration’s behaviour when it declared Ebrahim Rasool, South Africa’s ambassador to the US, persona non grata in March 2025 for comments he had made criticising Trump. Unfortunately for Pretoria, this has been interpreted in Washington as weakness, and it has given greater impetus to its determination to bring an errant South Africa to heel. The Bozell appointment confirmed the Trump administration’s overt hostility – and that of its support base – to a post-1994 democratic South Africa which, it is worth noting, would not exist at all had Bozell’s approach prevailed. South Africa is viewed by Washington as a standard bearer for the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion policies so loathed by this administration. Its opposition to the US attacks on Iran in 2025-26 and the genocide case it has brought against Israel before the International Court of Justice have only deepened the antagonism. Stormy waters On Ambassador Bozell’s watch, US-South Africa relations are set to deteriorate further as a confrontational relationship now seems to be Washington’s objective. This was confirmed on November 2 by its decision to remove South Africa from the US African Growth and Opportunity Act of 2000 under which many products from African states enjoy duty free access to the American market US removes South Africa from Agoa trade pact. That expulsion will take effect from January 2027. True, South Africa is not unique among contemporary democracies in having its sovereignty persistently challenged and undermined by the current US administration. Brazil, Canada, Denmark, Germany, Poland, Romania, Spain, and Ukraine have all found themselves at the sharp end of this established pattern of US interference and coercion The U.S. Is Bullying Europe Like Never Before – The Atlantic. However, in a world where we are witnessing genocidal violence in Gaza, Myanmar, Sudan, and Ukraine, the Trump administration has chosen to identify South Africa as an adversary deserving of special opprobrium and punitive sanctions. This is a South Africa which, despite its many failings and huge challenges, has a robust democratic infrastructure with regular free elections (its latest municipal elections were held on 4 November), an admirable constitution, a free press, a thriving civil society, and an independent judiciary. That it has become the target of such deep and sustained US hostility perhaps tells us more about the Trump administration than it does about contemporary South Africa.

author: Othmane El Jadid
title: Morocco’s Generation of Disillusionment: Bread and Circuses, and a Generation Left Waiting
content:
A year since GenZ 212 took to the streets of Morocco, it is a calmer place. We’ve all had our elections, and a new government in place. However, many questions remain. The most difficult one that comes to mind is… what happened to the generation?




The Autumn We’ll Never Forget




With Morocco preparing to host the Africa Cup of Nations, Autumn 2025 was an exciting time. However, many young Moroccans were starting to ask the question… what about us?




GenZ 212 – referring to Morocco’s telephone country code – started online, but the message quickly spread to the streets demanding better healthcare, quality education, jobs, ending corruption and living with dignity.




With news of , the anger was sparked. How could Morocco really fail to provide basic public services with the country preparing to invite the world?




On the 26h October 2025, I wrote a post on social media reflecting on the Roman phrase ‘Panem et Circenses’ meaning ‘give them bread and circuses.’ This was a reflection on how we can become too caught up in the spectacle of our country. Whilst we can create amazing stadiums and organise tournaments to impress the world, what does it matter if we can’t get appropriate care in hospitals or quality opportunities after years of education? I couldn’t have predicted how relevant this would be a year later.




The Voices That Were Silenced

author: Sleshi Teshome Kehali
title: The Bone-Setters’ Ward: How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia’s Modern Healthcare Vacuum
content:
Reporting from Bahir Dar, Ethiopia




In a residential neighbourhood of Bahir Dar, in northwestern Ethiopia, patients visit the home of W/ro Birqe Yibre for help with injuries. Birqe, a traditional bone-setter known locally as a Wogesha, has practised for more than 20 years.




W/ro Birqe Yibre, a traditional bone-setter known locally as a Wogesha, sits in her residential courtyard in Bahir Dar, Ethiopia. She says she has practised for more than two decades. (Photo: Sleshi Teshome)




One of her patients, Yidersal Mengistu, came with a painful right foot and a bruised big toe after kicking a stone while playing football.




“I didn’t go to the hospital. To be honest, I prefer the traditional way,” Mengistu said. He explained that he had visited Birqe before for heel pain and believed her treatment had helped him. He also said she had treated him without charge on that earlier occasion.




“If I recover fully this time, I will pay her,” he said.




For Birqe, payment depends partly on what patients can afford. She said people who have money typically pay between 150 and 200 Ethiopian birr, while she treats those who cannot pay without charging them.




“If someone has no money, I treat them and tell them, ‘Go on, go home,’” she said. “You cannot turn away poor people.”

BMC Complementary M

author: Francesco Rota
title: FILM AFRICA Press Release
content:
The Royal African Society Announces the Successful Conclusion of the 2026 Film Africa Festival




London, United Kingdom,  9th November 2026




The Royal African Society is delighted to announce the successful conclusion of its 125

th

 Anniversary edition of Film Africa Festival which took place from 23 October to 1 November.

 Now in its 13

th

 year, Film Africa celebrated the richness, diversity, and creativity of African cinema and brought together audiences, filmmakers, industry professionals, and supporters for an inspiring celebration of African storytelling. The festival screened 38 films from 30 African countries, and hosted two symposia, across 11 venues in London, Sheffield, Bristol, and Plymouth.




The festival provided a vibrant platform for African filmmakers to share compelling stories, highlighted diverse perspectives, and engaged audiences through the power of film. This year’s Film Africa Festival provided a special focus on

 The Role of African Women in Cinema, and the Importance of Sustainable Finance, Intellectual Property and Digital Technology 

for the future of African Cinema.

author: Rishika Pardikar
title: African Arguments Interview with Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah Ahead of COP31
content:
The 31st climate talks (COP31) began in Antalya, 

Türkiye 

on 9 November

. 

The African Group of Negotiators (AGN), an alliance of all of the 54 countries from the continent, had submitted three agenda proposals to the UNFCCC for the conference. One concerned a demand to triple adaptation finance, the other related to trade-related climate measures like carbon border taxes and the last one was about financing arrangements under the Green Climate Fund (GCF), a climate fund established under the UNFCCC to assist developing countries in mitigation and adaptation. None of the three proposals made it into the final agenda adopted for COP31. However, the COP31 presidents said negotiation tracks concerned with trade-related climate measures and the GCF will take the respective matters under consideration during negotiations in the following days. If the proposals by AGN were accepted, all three themes would have been negotiated as separate agenda items in their own right. 




Nevertheless, the fact that AGN made three submissions shows that the bloc seeks to assert its voice on the global stage.

author: Lovin Kobusingye
title: Africa Can’t Build a Blue Economy Without the Women Who Bring Its Fish to Market
content:
Before dawn, wherever Africa has a coast or a lake, women wait on the shore for the boats. When the catch lands, our work begins. We smoke, dry, salt or ferment the fish, using skills passed down for generations, and carry it to market. We are more than a quarter of the 

12.3 million people

 who work in Africa’s fisheries, and 

58 percent

 of its fish processors.




In July, African ministers meeting in Luanda promised women, youth and local communities at least 

40 percent representation

 in blue economy advisory bodies and financing programmes. The African Union Commission has been tasked with drafting the roadmap to deliver it. Unless that roadmap names women fish processors and traders, and removes the rules that keep us from credit, the promise will pass us by.







 




Many countries still count fisheries only by what happens in the water, so the millions of women who process and trade the catch barely register. But if you are invisible, you receive invisible budgets, invisible investments and invisible policies.




I am one of these women. I run a fish-processing business in Uganda, where our lakes yield more than half a million tonnes of fish a year, more than any other African country’s inland waters. author: Fabrizio Floris
title: Paying to work: bribery and the earnings of Kenya’s informal workers
content:
For many informal workers in Kenya, earning a living also means paying for the right to do so. A motorbike taxi rider, a hawker or a small trader may be asked for money by a police officer or a county inspector. It is not a tax set by law, nor necessarily a fine for an offence. It is an informal payment that becomes part of the daily conditions of running a business. According to the 

World Bank

, informal workers can lose up to 20 percent of their daily earnings this way.




The figure appears in the 

Kenya Economic Update

 published on 4 November 2026, which 

looks at how weak governance holds back growth and job creation

. The report describes a country that keeps growing but where growth struggles to improve living conditions: GDP expanded by 5.2 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, yet 83.8 percent of workers are in the informal economy, where incomes are unstable and protection is thin.




It is worth being clear about where the 20 percent comes from. In the body of the report, the most detailed estimate concerns motorbike riders: sources cited put bribes at between 5 and 20 percent of daily earnings, or KSh 50 to 100 a day, with occasional larger demands on top. author: Abdulbagi Mohammad
title: Formalising the RSF: EU Policies and Sudan’s Search for Funds
content:
The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) are one of the two armed parties in the current war in Sudan. Despite their historic collaborations with multiple domestic and external actors, everyone is washing their hands of them. In this piece, I will try to make sense of the RSF and conclude by associating its institutionalisation with the convergence of goals between Sudan and the EU in the 2010s.




It depends on where you stand to identify the root causes of the formalisation and institutionalisation of the RSF. In 2003, when the war broke out in Darfur, Sudan’s western region, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) received a 

humiliating shock

. The Sudanese government then mobilised Darfurians, who know the geography of the area and who were mobile enough to cope with the insurgents’ tactics. The rebel groups were mostly from non-Arab ancestries, while the bulk of the counterinsurgent militias were Darfurian Arabs including Mohammad Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’ (the current leader of RSF) and others. The counterinsurgency campaign was successful militarily, but against the backdrop of this ‘‘succes’’ the campaign left damaging results. in March 2009

author: Eibhlin Priestley
title: After the Revolution, Before the War: Tracing Khartoum’s Syrian Community
content:
On 18 March 2023, Arwa Ahmed, an architect, and photographer of the Sudanese revolution, and I stood chatting in the shade of the Grand Hotel on Nile Street in Khartoum. We had spent the morning jumping in and out of Arwa’s white Hyundai photographing buildings of historic significance for the Syrian community. The quiet of the afternoon was broken as ten trucks, each holding dozens of men in civilian dress drove past us at speed. It was an unusual sight, one that we commented on at the time. Less than a month later, we would realise these men were fighters from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) bussed into Khartoum to battle the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) unleashing hell on the people of Sudan on 15 April 2023. The country has since suffered what UNHCR has described as the most devastating humanitarian and displacement crisis in the world, largely out of sight of media attention.




Entrance to the Grand Hotel, Nile Street, a popular choice for Syrian weddings in the 1950s and 1960s. Photo by Arwa Ahmed.




Eighteen months into my History PhD, I arrived in Khartoum in March 2023 to meet and interview members of the Syrian community whose grandparents or great-grandparents arrived in Sudan from Greater Syria (today’s Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, and Jordan) at the turn of the twentieth century. author: Joseph Sampson
title: Who Decides What Africa Reads First?
content:
Every morning, someone decides what Africa reads first.




Usually it is not one person. Often it is not a person at all. It is a recommendation algorithm tuned for engagement, a foreign desk deciding which of fifty-four countries deserves a slot today…or a cousin who forwards a voice note to the family WhatsApp group before breakfast.




The continent has no shortage of journalism. What it lacks is a shared front page. And the question of who assembles one, and how, deserves more attention than it gets.




I was born in Ghana and live in the United States, but my relationship with newspapers started very early. My older cousins still brag that I started reading newspapers when I was only six years old. I vaguely remember the age, but I clearly remember the scene.




In 1986, our 15-inch black-and-white family TV was stolen. Overnight, the house went quiet. For entertainment, for company, for anything to do after school, all I had were the newspapers my uncle brought home from work. He would come in with a stack of papers, and I would spread them across the living room floor, sit in the middle and read the 

Daily Graphic, Ghanaian Times

, the weekend 

Spectator

 and the 

Mirror

 from front to back. I feasted on everything. In the early 1990s, when 

The Ghanaian Chronicle

 arrived, I especially waited for whatever the late Paul Ansah wrote. If he wrote it, I read it.

author: Florence Kyei
title: Who Pays When the Applause Stops? Visibility, Power and Ghana’s Black Challenge
content:
The Black Challenge has won African titles, an African Para Games gold medal and a place at the 2026 Amputee Football World Cup. Yet weeks before leaving for Mexico, where they will face Angola, Colombia and Iraq in Group D, Ghana’s national amputee football team is still appealing for financial support.




This is the paradox at the heart of Ghanaian para-football: a team successful enough to bring international recognition and national pride, but not yet supported by a sporting system strong enough to make that success sustainable.




The appeal came at 

the team’s unveiling in Accra on September 28

, where the president of the National Paralympic Committee Ghana (NPC-Ghana), Samson Deen, called on the government to settle outstanding bonuses and per diems and allocate at least 5% of the Black Stars budget to amputee football.




At the same event, 

NPC-Ghana announced bonuses of GH¢10,000 for each player and GH¢5,000 for each official

 under its “Target the Podium” initiative.




Deen also said the Black Challenge “deserves everything that sports winners win for the nation.”







The issue predates the current World Cup campaign. In May 2024, captain Richard Arthur Opentil 

publicly raised concerns about outstanding bonuses and inadequate support

 while the team competed at the Amputee Africa Cup of Nations in Cairo.

author: Goktug Caliskan
title: A Russian state firm will map more than half of Mali. Who will own the data?
content:
Two contracts signed in Moscow give a Russian state firm the job of mapping Mali’s subsoil and building the system that will hold the data. The accounts published so far do not say who will own it.




On 28 October, at the Russia–Africa summit in Moscow, Mali’s Mines Minister, Amadou Keïta, signed 

two contracts

 with Zarubezhgeologia, the foreign-projects arm of the state-owned geological holding Rosgeologia, also known as Rosgeo. The first commissioned geological maps at a scale of 

1:200,000

 of two areas that together cover more than half of Mali, over 24 months. The second, scheduled for eight months, purchased a national geological information system called “Subsoil Management”.




The mapping includes training for staff of Mali’s National Directorate of Geology and Mines. Reuters, relaying the company’s statement, says the information system is meant to let Mali manage geological data, mineral licensing and regulatory oversight. Other reports describe only spatial storage with tools to visualise and analyse the data.




Bamako’s partnership with Moscow has mostly been read through security, from the arrival of Wagner in 

late 2021

 to the Africa Corps, which has operated under Russia’s Defence Ministry since last year. These contracts reach somewhere else: the records of the Ministry of Mines.

author: Carine Kaneza Nantulya
title: Kenya’s 2027 Election: Time to Address the Warning Signs
content:
On August 16, 2026, hundreds of people armed with machetes, guns, and sticks 

attacked

 a convoy carrying opposition politicians and supporters of the Linda Mwananchi movement in Homa Bay county, western Kenya. The attackers killed at least three people and beat and robbed journalists covering the violence. Witnesses said police officers were present but failed to contain the attacks. The incident was among 

a series of violent attacks targeting civil society events and opposition gatherings

 in the months leading up to Kenya’s August 10, 2027, general elections. At least six people have reportedly been killed and dozens injured in these attacks, raising serious concerns about the safety of political participation as the campaign season gathers pace.







I returned to Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, where my colleagues and I have been speaking with people from different walks of life to understand how they view the political and human rights environment ahead of the 2027 elections for president and the National Assembly. President William Ruto is expected to seek a second term, while opposition parties and candidates have already begun mobilizing supporters at rallies across the country.

title: Nigeria’s AI Ambitions vs. The Regulatory Void–Who Protects the Citizens?
content:
Last year, scammers launched a deepfake videos of popular Nigerian social media influencer, 

Martins Vincent Otse

, through a fraudulent Facebook campaign. The cybercriminals superimposed a fabricated AI-generated audio on a genuine video of Otse from early 2024.




Martins Vincent Otse




In the cloned voice, Otse introduced an online chatting scheme where viewers could earn up to $1,000 monthly. By cloning the influencer’s face and reputation, the scammers not only harmed Otse’s reputation as a respected influencer, they also preyed on the poverty of many Nigerians, tricking them into becoming a member of an online platform created to appropriate their personal information and savings.




On 

October 5

, to show that the issue still mattered, the Nigeria Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) warned organisations and staff against sharing sensitive data with public AI tools.

author: Huyam Salih and Obai Khalifa
title: Africa cannot build a stronger agrifood economy while the livestock sector loses $4 billion a year
content:
Across Africa, the livestock sector supports more than 350 million people. Livestock is much more than an agricultural commodity. For millions of families, cattle, sheep, goats, poultry, and other animals are sources of food and income. They are also productive assets that support trade, processing, services, employment and rural wealth creation. Despite its centrality to Africa’s wider agrifood economy, the systems that govern and influence the continent’s livestock sector remain among the most undercapitalised parts of African agriculture. Africa loses an estimated USD 4 billion every year due to unrealised livestock potential.




Too often, livestock farmers, particularly pastoralists and small-scale producers, are seen through the lens of subsistence and poverty. Investors see fragmented markets, climate exposure and informal production systems and conclude that the risks are too high. The challenge is therefore not only a shortage of capital, but an investability gap: fragmented supply, weak market information, uncertain offtake, and policy and regulatory uncertainty can make otherwise viable opportunities difficult to assess and finance.

author: Paula Slier
title: The War in Sudan and the Challenges of Mediation
content:
Less than two months after Sudan’s war began in April 2023, the then African Union (AU) Commission chair, Moussa Faki Mahamat, called it the ‘prototype’ for ‘African solutions to African problems’.




More than three years later, some of the most consequential diplomacy is taking place through processes that extend well beyond the continent: in Jeddah, Washington and through the Quad of the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt.




Africa has not been absent. On 23 September, the current AU Commission chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, co-chaired with US envoy Massad Boulos the first joint meeting of the Quad and Quintet. The Quintet brings together the AU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the United Nations, European Union and the League of Arab States.




So the question is not where Africa is. It is why African diplomacy has struggled to make more of a difference. Part of the answer lies in the African mediation itself: competing initiatives and disagreements over who should lead and how the war should be handled. But there is another problem that no mediator has yet managed to overcome.

author: Albashir Dahab
title: Delayed Rains and Broken Routes: War and Climate Crisis in North Darfur’s Jebel Issa
content:
All names of individuals interviewed for this article have been changed their safety and privacy. 




The Fatal Rain of Wadi Saleh




In mid-September 2026, when rain finally touched the parched soil of Jebel Issa in North Darfur’s Al-Malha locality, it did not bring life, but rather severe ecological and economic devastation.




Under normal conditions along this fragile Sahelian belt, the rainy season begins in mid-June or early July and extends through late September This predictable precipitation serves as the ultimate lifeline for rainfed millet and sorghum farming, as well as the primary water source for livestock grazing across the northern Darfur plains. This year, however, unprecedented climate variability left the skies dry until 12 September.




When a sudden isolated downpour finally struck the western sectors of Jebel Issa livestock already severely weakened by months of starvation, scorching heat, and gruelling treks between depleted pastures and distant wells suffered immediate thermal and physical shock. Over three consecutive days, from 12 to 14 September, more than 420 head of sheep perished in Wadi Saleh alone, with additional unrecorded livestock deaths reported across neighbouring valleys.

title: Laying on Thin Water: The Looming Danger of Sub-Saharan Africa’s Subsea Repair Vessel Deficit
content:
Submarine fibre-optic cables (subsea telecommunications cables) handle up to 

99%

 of our global internet traffic and communications, underlining the operations of numerous businesses and institutions across the world. Their continued proliferation will bring higher network speeds and connect more people and regions to digital communications. Yet, whilst the world is on a roll in laying down more of this critical infrastructure, it is severely underequipped in properly maintaining them. Sub-Saharan Africa is no exception. As the region with the 

fastest-growing population

 and a 

large gap

 to fill in terms of internet connectivity, Sub-Saharan Africa is occupying an increasingly important position in the world’s network of submarine fibre-optic cables.
